Environmental stressors, urban design and planning:
implications for human behaviour and health
Giyoung Parka and Gary W. Evansb
aDepartment of Design and environmental analysis, Cornell university, ithaca, usa; bDepartments of Design
and environmental analysis and of Human Development, bronfenbrenner Center for Translational research,
Cornell university, ithaca, usa
ABSTRACT
Urban and neighbourhood design can moderate the effects of
building design on human behaviour and well-being, and vice versa.
The interdependence between built environments across scales is
critical yet is often poorly understood. This paper overviews several
psychological processes linking human behaviour to environmental
design, both inside and out. In particular, the paper focuses on two
environmental stressors ‒ crowding and noise ‒ in four daily indoor
environments: residential, school, work and commuting. These
two stressors are often linked and can adversely impact people if
improperly designed. Moreover, urban and neighbourhood design
can mitigate such negative effects. Key suggestions for practitioners
and policy makers include proper acoustic design, easily accessible
semi-public or outdoor places and walkable streets. Some illustrations
of the nexus between neighbourhood and building design show that
the tendency of research traditions in environment and behaviour
to focus on one scale of environmental design probably misses
important human-environment transactions.
Introduction
The aim of this paper is to bridge the knowledge gap between urban design and planning
and environmental psychology. Instead of dichotomizing in- and outside of buildings, the
paper summarizes studies of crowding and noise in four indoor settings and discusses build-
ing and urban design. Psychologists traditionally use laboratory settings to control environ-
mental variables in order to isolate the causal effect of a singular variable on human
behaviour. This makes it difficult for designers and planners to use psychological insights in
practice because their interests lie in the total context of the setting or space they are design-
ing. In addition, for designers and planners, other factors – such as economy or aesthetics
– are often prioritized in practice. Furthermore, the critical experience of transitions over
time and across settings that are fundamental to human experience of places is often given
inadequate attention in environment and empirical research.
The bioecological model illustrates how recurrent interactions between an individual and
both proximal interior and more distal settings can shape a person’s development over time

(Bronfenbrenner 1993; Bronfenbrenner and Morris 2006). This model is not a product of
environmental determinism but takes into account both individuals’ traits (e.g. gender, per-
sonality) and surrounding environments. Given the focus of this paper, the environmental
aspects of the framework are discussed. Environments encompass physical settings, social
dynamics and socio-cultural factors (Figure 1a). Settings wherein we spend more time on a
regular basis probably create greater impacts on our lives. Furthermore, a person’s interaction
in an environment not only influences their development and well-being but also creates
spillover effects across settings. For example, a caregiver’s mood after work may indirectly
influence an adolescent’s well-being (Figure 1b) (Tisdale and Pitt-Catsuphes 2011). More
examples of spillover effects are discussed later in this paper.
Increasingly, environmental psychologists are realizing the importance of not only the
intensity of exposure (e.g. sound levels) but also duration. This is important theoretically and
practically. From a theoretical perspective, consideration of temporal dimensions of exposure
provides insight into how human beings respond when confronted with suboptimal settings.
From a practical standpoint, research on the importance of setting exposure timing can be
translated into, for example, public-transportation planning for shorter commute times. as
of 2014, 54% of the world’s population lives in urban areas and the percentage is increasing
(The United nations 2014). Time spent indoors, including time in transportation, exceeds
90% among Europeans and north americans (US EPa 1989; European Union 2003). asian
children spend more time indoors than those in other cultures (Morgan, Ohno-Matsui, and
Saw 2012). This pattern has been found to be consistent even among Chinese-ethnic children
in Singapore and Sydney (rose et al. 2008). Considering the significant amounts of time
people spend in the built environment, understanding its influence on human behaviour is
important for research, design practice, planning and policy. Crowding and noise are among
important environmental stressors occurring frequently in daily life and are directly relevant
to planners and designers. Therefore, this paper reviews these two processes in four indoor
settings ‒ home, school, office and commuting ‒ to examine the influence of the built

environment on human behaviour and health. Office settings, instead of workplace in gen-
eral, are discussed because over 50% of the modern workforce in developed countries works
in office settings (duffy and Powell 1997). Office settings may differ from other workplace
types, but the paper can provide a basic understanding of crowding and noise in other work
settings. Finally, commuting is included because it is more often unpleasant than other daily
activities (Kahneman and Krueger 2006). additional evidence of stress in commuting is also
included later in the paper.
Studies written in English using human subjects were reviewed primarily using Google
Scholar. For crowding, crowding, density, residential crowding, classroom crowding, workplace
crowding, crowding in office, privacy in office, office type and commute crowding were searched.
For noise, chronic noise, environmental noise, residential noise, residential noise and children,
noise and blood pressure, classroom noise, office noise, open office noise and transportation
noise and commute. The term stress was added to some of the terms listed above for more
specific results. In addition, neighbourhood quality was used because it can exacerbate or
buffer the effects of immediate suboptimal settings. The paper did not exclude studies con-
ducted in other cultures; however, most studies reviewed were conducted in Western
countries.
Environmental stress
Stress arises when external demands exceed personal resources. Environmental features
including design elements at both the building and community scale can produce stress;
environmental stressors (e.g. crowding, noise) are often chronic and uncontrollable. Chronic,
unpredictable and uncontrollable stressors commonly produce adverse feelings while at
the same time elevating physiological response systems such as raising blood pressure or
stress hormone levels; these reactions reduce an individual’s ability to carry out complex
tasks (Bilotta and Evans 2013). When such stressors occur in primary environments where
individuals spend significant amounts of time, their impacts can be large.
Crowding
Having too much social interaction in a given situation is defined as crowding. It is a subjec-
tive measure of density that exceeds a person’s coping capacity and thus causes stress.
Crowding is different from density that is an objective measure of the number of people per
spatial units (e.g. people/km2 or /room) (Stokols 1972). animal and human studies show
detrimental physiological and behavioural outcomes of chronic crowding (Hall 1969). The
perception of high density varies by a person’s socio-cultural1 and individual factors as well
as type of settings (e.g. night clubs vs. residential). as crowding involves the perceived density
of a person’s immediate area, and because people spend most of their days indoors, interior
density (e.g. the number of people per room), rather than external density (e.g. people per
km2), is the key density metric that affects human behaviour and social support (Evans 2001,
2006). In fact, research on areal measures of density find little or no evidence of stress but
some positive yet modest impacts on social interaction and physical activity. In workplace
studies, the term privacy is more commonly used. In psychology, privacy is a process opti-
mizing the amount of social interactions, thus involving both access to people and ability
to reduce unwanted interactions (altman 1976). Over-achieved social interaction leads to

456 G. ParK and G. W. EvanS
crowding and interferes with privacy. Workplace studies that consider the aspects of crowd-
ing were selected, rather than the ones of workplace privacy only in terms of confidentiality
or private information securement.
Noise
Similar to crowding and density, noise is defined as unwanted sound and can be contrasted
with sound intensity. loud, unpredictable and chronic sound, such as aircraft and construc-
tion noise, are more annoying (Glass and Singer 1972). The same sound may be perceived
differently by different people, or by the same person in different contexts (e.g. loud music
at bedtime vs. at a concert). In addition to hearing loss, noise can cause non-auditory effects,
including hypertension, sleep disturbance, increased psychological distress, and impaired
cognitive development and memory, which is in line with stress-response outcomes (WHO
1999; Clark and Stansfeld 2007; van Kamp and davies 2013). Influential noise variables
include sound types, duration of exposure (both per incidence and length of residence),
settings (e.g. residence vs. school, work vs. recreation), environmental quality (e.g. acoustic
design) and individual sensitivity. In addition, greater noise levels decreased helping behav-
iour explaining less altruism in urban areas (Cohen and Spacapan 1984).
Soundscape is also a concept that illustrates the auditory quality of settings. The reduction
or elimination of noise does not necessarily improve soundscape (raimbault and dubois
2005). Human-generated sounds (e.g. conversation, music, walking) contribute to lively
urban and neighbourhood space (raimbault and dubois 2005; Brambilla, Gallo, and Zambon
2013); however, they may become stressors indoors (Enmarker and Boman 2004; Kearns et
al. 2012). Traffic sound damages the soundscape of both interiors and exteriors whereas
preference for natural sound is consistent across studies (raimbault and dubois 2005). High
traffic noise is associated with low perceived safety as well as with high residential mobility
or transient areas (appleyard 1981).
Home
residential crowding harms mental health and can spill over into behaviours in other set-
tings, even those that are not crowded. learned helplessness reflects a residual impact fol-
lowing exposure to uncontrollable stressors (Seligman 1972). learned helplessness may
occur in crowded settings given less controllable social interaction. american elementary
schoolchildren from an urban low-income, minority community and from a white, rural
community in the State of new York showed increased learned helplessness in relation to
elevated household density (Evans, Saegert, and Harris 2001). learned helplessness was
assessed in the laboratory by a standard behavioural protocol using task persistence on
challenging, age-appropriate puzzles. Children’s externalizing behaviours increased with
household density only among boys in the same study. This may reflect males’ greater per-
sonal space relative to females’ (aiello 1987). Similarly, high household density was associated
with boys’ high blood pressure and with girls’ learned helplessness among Indian school-
children (Evans et al. 1998), and laboratory studies show similar trends for multiple physio-
logical stress measures (aiello 1987). residential crowding impairs children’s cognitive
development. Individuals try to minimize the surfeit of social interaction that happens in
the close presence of too many people. Unfortunately, this response also leads parents in

JOUrnal OF UrBan dESIGn 457
crowded households to socially withdraw at home, leading to lower amounts and complexity
of parent-to-child communication and reduced parental responsiveness to children (Wachs
1989). This, in turn, mediates the direct effect of crowding on children’s cognitive develop-
ment (crowding  lower parental responsiveness  diminished cognitive development)
(Evans and Saegert 2000). One limitation in some of these studies is the prescriptive temporal
sequence: crowding  diminished parent-child interaction  adverse child outcomes, has
typically been investigated in cross-sectional studies. a more rigorous approach would assess
the environmental factor at time 1, the moderator at time 2 and the child outcomes at
time 3.
In addition, residential density (people/room) can interact with house type. Interact means
that the relation between the stressor (crowding in this example) and human reactions varies
as a function of some other factor, which is house type in the present example. Mental health
was worse for children living in more crowded large multi-dwelling units compared to those
in more crowded single-family houses and row houses controlling for social class (Evans,
lercher, and Kofler 2002). recent research has also suggested that neighbourhood quality
can moderate housing characteristic to change its impacts on residents (Jones-rounds,
Evans, and Braubach 2014). less accessible outdoor spaces and fewer opportunities for
solitude in multi-dwelling units could exacerbate crowding and create more undesirable
and uncontrollable social interaction. Shorter hallway corridors in college dormitory build-
ings reduced perceived crowding compared to long hallway corridors, holding room area
constant (Baum and davis 1980). Self-reported as well as observed social interaction in these
same dormitories showed greater social withdrawal in the long- compared to short-corridor
hallways controlling for the numbers of residents per floor and other physical variables.
Interestingly, a study of high-rise dwellings linked noise with crowding (Kearns et al. 2012).
residents who lived in six-storey or higher buildings noted dissatisfaction with their home
due to inter-unit noise compared to those living in a non-high-rise flat or a single-family
house. Unfortunately, measures of building size, unit layout or sound attenuation properties
were not included in the study. Therefore, it is unknown whether crowding itself exacerbates
noise or not. Inter-unit noise might reflect the unwanted presence of others even though
they were not in the same room. Few studies have examined indoor-generated noise in
residential settings.
The effects of chronic noise may vary by the age of exposure. Children chronically exposed
to high noise levels (e.g. proximal to airports or major roads) appear to learn to tune out
auditory stimuli, not only traffic noise but other auditory stimuli, including speech (Cohen
et al. 1986). These children have deficits in auditory discrimination, for example, are these
two words when presented orally, ‘boat’ and ‘goat’, the same or different? This in turn mediates
the well-documented adverse impacts of noise exposure on reading acquisition. Speech
perception or phonological awareness is a fundamental building block of reading acquisition.
Several large longitudinal studies, including the los angeles and Munich airport noise stud-
ies, ranCH (road traffic and aircraft noise exposure and children’s cognition and health) and
HYEna (hypertension and exposure to noise near airports), have shown adverse impacts of
transportation noise levels on blood pressure in children and adults (Clark and Stansfeld
2007). noise effects on children’s mental health are much less clear with some studies finding
no impacts or limited to certain outcomes such as children’s hyperactivity (Stansfeld et al.
2005, 2009). Children living near Munich airport reported a significantly lower quality of life
after the airport opened relative to pre-opening levels and compared to their peers in nearby

458 G. ParK and G. W. EvanS
towns that remained quiet (Evans, Bullinger, and Hygge 1998). In the HYEna study, night-
time aircraft noise elevated blood pressure in adults who had lived in the same residence
five years or longer, while road traffic noise increased male but not female blood pressure
(Jarup et al. 2008). age interacted with gender and noise levels on adults’ blood pressure.
Similarly, in Sweden those who had lived at the same residence over 10 years showed
stronger effects (Bluhm et al. 2007). note the importance not only of noise levels but also
duration of exposures in these transportation noise studies.
It should be noted that nearly all of these noise and children’s reading studies using large
samples pre-screened for normal auditory activity and relied on noise assessment data such
as leq(a) contour maps around airports or busy roads without adjusting for individual-level
environmental variables. Given the amount of time people spend indoors, insufficient adjust-
ment for building attributes and household density, as well as reliance on external noise
levels from sound contour maps, might lead to imprecise estimates of actual exposures. Few
residential-noise studies measure indoor sound levels; others use indirect adjustments such
as bedroom and living room locations, window glazing and window opening habits, house-
hold crowding, soundscapes, single-family houses vs. multi-dwelling units, and other indi-
vidual-level variables (e.g. Bluhm et al. 2007; Pujol et al. 2013). More ecologically valid noise
exposure may provide more precise noise-human effect data (lercher et al. 2011). Somewhat
surprisingly, little is known about sound attenuation of traffic noise. Scant research has
looked into the effects of sound barrier walls on annoyance, and none have examined their
potential mitigation on cognitive functions or physiological responses.
School
Crowding in school can be influential. Class size is the number of the students in a classroom
taught by a teacher, which is different from pupil/teacher ratio that is the number of students
in a school divided by the number of teachers and staff. Project STar (Student/Teacher
achievement ratio) in Tennessee, US, monitored a large sample of kindergarteners from
approximately 100 schools randomly assigned to class sizes of 13–17 students or 22–26
students. Students remained in the same class until they returned to regular classrooms at
4th grade. Students who stayed in smaller-sized classes for three years or longer showed
greater academic achievement, less classroom disruption and greater high school graduation
rates (Finn, Gerber, and Boyd-Zaharias 2005). These positive outcomes did not occur among
students who were in larger classes, including those with an assistant teacher. The difference
in high school graduation rates between small class sizes and the other conditions were
more significant among low-income students. It is unknown how household crowding inter-
acted with school crowding in this study. Both high daycare-centre and residential densities
can interact to influence pre-schoolers’ performance and behaviour (Maxwell 1996). Smaller
area per student in the classroom lowers girls’ reading performance while boys were not
influenced noticeably in two urban elementary schools (Maxwell 2003). note that both
loudness and qualitative aspects of noise, such as speech properties, are important.
noise can interfere with cognitive functioning. Speech and transportation noise are
important environmental noise sources. Human-generated indoor sounds, such as classroom
chatter and table or chair scraping can annoy both students and, to a greater extent, teachers
more than street noise in areas with moderate exterior sound levels (Enmarker and Boman
2004). Both road traffic noise and meaningful irrelevant speech decreased adult long-term

JOUrnal OF UrBan dESIGn 459
memory (Hygge, Boman, and Enmarker 2003; Enmarker 2004; Boman, Enmarker, and Hygge
2005). Irrelevant speech, but not road traffic noise, was also detrimental for recognition
memory among adults over 35 (Enmarker 2004).
Chronic exposure to aircraft noise has consistently showed negative effects on children’s
reading (Evans 2006). Chronic exposure to aircraft noise at home lowers levels of 9–10-year-
old children’s reading comprehension in a linear manner while road traffic was insignificant
(Clark and Stansfeld 2007). Chronic exposure to higher street noise at school impaired 8- and
9-year-old children’s language and mathematics test scores. noise at home in the evening
and at night was associated with both language and mathematics scores. However, when
combined with school noise levels, residential noise levels became marginally significant
(Pujol et al. 2013). School noise levels negatively influenced elementary students’ academic
performance, including mathematics and reading, with stronger effects among older stu-
dents (Shield and dockrell 2008). To give some sense of the magnitude of impact, one of
the largest studies of aircraft noise and reading indicates a 20 decibel increase in noise levels
is equivalent to a 0.2 standard deviation decrease or a delay of two months in reading per-
formance among 2nd-grade children (Klatte et al. 2016). However, once children reach sec-
ondary school, noise exposure may not produce any additional damage (Xie, Kang, and
Tompsett 2011). This pattern of results indicates that in addition to duration of exposure,
the developmental timing of noise exposure may also be important in thinking about human
impacts of environmental quality. Furthermore, a field study found higher street noise level
at a residence and at school lowered teacher-rated primary schoolchildren’s executive func-
tioning, but only among boys (Belojević et al. 2012). note that K-12 schools are close to
home; thus, transportation and street noise exposure probably occur both in residences and
in school. Similar to residential noise studies, most transportation noise studies using school
settings use sound contour maps instead of sound level in classrooms. a Swedish study
found higher sound levels during school hours leads to higher cortisol levels among
4th-grade students, indicating greater stress levels compared to low sound level days, but
no effects on blood pressure or pulse rates (Wålinder et al. 2007).
Office
Workplace studies use the term privacy ‒ optimizing the amount of social interaction ‒ more
often than crowding. Casual encounters in the office are essential in informal training, inter-
disciplinary work and team building (Becker 2007). Employees working in traditional private
offices often desire a greater amount of social interaction while those in open offices prob-
ably experience crowding and noise (Haynes 2008; danielsson 2010; Kim and de dear 2013).
Typical workstation configurations in the US and many other countries are 4 ft x 6 ft (equiv-
alent to 1.2 m x 1.8 m) or larger; therefore, area per person is far greater in school and home
settings. despite the greater opportunities of social encounters plus seemingly sufficient
individual workspaces, open office layouts interfere with performance and are rated lower
than private cellular offices across studies (Kim and de dear 2013). Until recently, organiza-
tions and researchers have favoured the former, underestimating crowding and noise. Social
interactions at work can aid cross-pollination and productivity; on the other hand, being
able to be alone or to reduce sensory inputs are also essential (Cain 2012). Irrelevant speech
and ambient noise are more of a concern in studies of office environments than street or
transportation noise. Moreover, high indoor sound levels interact with job strain, aggravating

460 G. ParK and G. W. EvanS
the negative effects of high job strain on employees’ psychological and physical well-being
(leather, Beale, and Sullivan 2003).
a shared private office by two or three persons may provide sufficient social interaction
without increasing crowding or noise significantly (danielsson 2010; de Been and Beijer
2014). a combi-office does not have a clear spatial definition, but provides various additional
unassigned settings for team or individual work in addition to assigned individual workspace
(Haynes 2008; danielsson 2010; de Been and Beijer 2014). Furthermore, information tech-
nologies (e.g. email, virtual private network (vPn), laptops) enable flex-office or hoteling
systems, in which workstations are not assigned and available to any employee (Becker
2007). Studies of these new types of office design are limited, varying slightly in office types,
and have generated some positive yet mixed results. Other factors such as organization
culture or task demands need to be incorporated into future research on these new types
of hybrid offices. In addition, office studies focus on interior environments without consid-
eration of how they are nested within building types or neighbourhoods.
Commuting
Commuting time takes a smaller portion of the day than the three settings discussed earlier;
however, its negative effects on well-being should not be ignored. longer commuting time
is associated with higher commuting strain and lower life satisfaction (Kluger 1998;
Gatersleben and Uzzell 2007; Stutzer and Frey 2008). When the new York/new Jersey
Metropolitan Transit authority consolidated train routes to Manhattan, it eliminated the
need for transfers for some riders, which significantly shortened commute time. Train com-
muters’ salivary cortisol levels, self- and spousal-rated stress levels plus proofreading per-
formance, all improved after the consolidation (Wener and Evans 2011). Spousal rating
supports carryover effect of commute stress. The researchers replicated these results in a
true experiment as well, randomly assigning college students to different commuting routes.
Traffic congestion is also linked to crowding on roads (Taylor 1999). driving can be more
stressful than public transportation commutes, particularly when faced with traffic conges-
tion (Gatersleben and Uzzell 2007).
When a person’s personal space is invaded, people feel uncomfortable and try to increase
interpersonal distance. One of the ways humans regulate the amount of social interaction
with others is by adjusting interpersonal distance or personal space (Hall 1969). If no further
space is available, physiological stress elevates. new York train commuters avoided taking
the middle seats in the three-seat rows, even when they had to stand otherwise (McGeehan
2005). Moreover, passengers who sat at either end of the three-seat rows tried to thwart
others’ taking the middle seats by putting bags and other belongings on the open seats.
new York commuter-train riders’ cortisol levels were significantly higher when seated imme-
diately next to another passenger than otherwise (Evans and Wener 2007). In contrast, sub-
way trains in Seoul have seven-seat rows against windows, which offers equal accessibility
from the central circulation path across the seats and allows confederate middle-seat riders.
End seats are preferred if available, but unlike new York trains, middle seats are mostly taken
(Figures 2a and 2b). no studies have examined if this is due to train car design, familiarity
with very high-density residential life in urban Korea or cultural norms; however, a similar
pattern was found in the Google cafeteria where 10–12-people tables are easier for small
groups to take a portion (Turkle 2015). Future studies regarding seat design are encouraged.

noise in commutes can be significant. Sound levels inside metro trains and at platforms of
the nYC and San Francisco Bay area metro systems are high enough to cause hearing loss
(dinno, Powell, and King 2011). no studies about the relationships among sound levels,
durations and stress during commutes have been identified.
To summarize, exposure to crowding and noise can result in a wide range of negative,
stress-related outcomes. This paper has identified several underlying explanations of how
these environmental stresses adversely impact human behaviour and health. architectural
design can moderate some of the adverse impacts of high sound and high interior density
levels, but few studies have examined this topic. Higher illumination levels (Schiffenbauer
et al. 1977), greater architectural depth ‒ that is, the number of intervening rooms (Evans,
lepore, and Schroeder 1996), higher ceiling levels (Savinar 1975), shorter corridors in mul-
ti-dwelling units (Baum and davis 1980) and clear hierarchical sequencing of solitary to
group spaces (altman 1975) have all been shown to interact with interior density and reduce
human responses to crowding (Evans and McCoy 1998). Some of these design attributes are
applicable to urban design. For example, hierarchical sequence from private (e.g. residential)
to public space and a greater number of intervening semi-public spaces could buffer urban
stimuli when inside. However, unsuccessful semi-public indoor space such as hallways in
multi-dwelling units can be negative (Baum and davis 1980). Creating urban and neigh-
bourhood places to escape from crowded homes may support residents’ coping (Cattell et
al. 2008). In contrast to negative effects of internal residential crowding, greater external

462 G. ParK and G. W. EvanS
density in urban space makes streets more walkable, which has positive effects, as discussed
below. Both environmental psychology and design and planning research ought to more
thoroughly investigate design properties as potential moderators of environmental stress
effects. It is also critical for designers and planners to distinguish between interior and exte-
rior density.
Design and planning implementation
The remainder of this paper illustrates how good acoustic design and easy access to
semi-public space can reduce the negative effects of the two environmental stressors in
urban design and planning projects. In addition, urban street design, which has potential
to reduce crowding and noise effects, is briefly discussed (Table 1).
Acoustic design
Setting and sound types may moderate annoyance with noise. Background conversation
sound was less of concern in outdoor neighbourhoods than traffic noise (appleyard 1981).
However, it is the most consistently annoying noise source in schools and office settings
(Enmarker and Boman 2004; Becker 2007; danielsson 2010). acoustic design can be impor-
tant in primary environments, for example, open offices as well as open classrooms (see
Evans 2006 for studies about noise in open-plan classrooms). nursery children’s pre-reading
performance, language skills and vulnerability to learned helplessness all improved after

installing sound absorbent panels in classrooms that substantially reduced reverberation
time (Maxwell and Evans 2000). This childcare centre was not near any significant external
noise sources, but had poor interior acoustical properties because of the design of the space
and lack of textured surfaces that would diffuse sound. Carpet flooring in trains can decrease
interior sound levels while tunnels increase them (neitzel et al. 2009; dinno, Powell, and King
2011). Other building features such as double-pane windows and enhanced wall insulation
can reduce sound transmission. Such features can buffer noise from other rooms or units
within buildings as well as from outside.
Semi-public space
Semi-public space is for community or group members. Semi-public space can be either
indoors (e.g. shared living room in a college dormitory suite, mailroom in multi-dwelling
buildings) or outdoors (e.g. a gated tennis court in a multi-dwelling unit complex and a
community garden). While successful semi-public spaces, whether indoors or outdoors, foster
social interaction among residents, insufficient or unsuccessful semi-public space contributes
to crowding, resulting in social withdrawal, anti-social behaviour and diminished sense of
community (Fleming, Baum, and Singer 1985; Kearns et al. 2012).
The concept of regulation of social interaction is a particularly useful heuristic for design-
ing spaces to support social interaction and minimize stress (altman 1973). designers and
planners can allocate multiple semi-public spaces to foster a gradient of privacy from inside
private homes to an outdoor public space. Multi-unit residential buildings often lack high
quality semi-public spaces, which brings about unwanted social interactions with other
residents (Gibson et al. 2011). Multiple amenities (e.g. mailboxes, bike racks, community
garden) allocated adjacent to major pathways, whether indoors or outdoors, can reinforce
social space for residents (Figure 3).
The idea of having amenities together can be applicable to neighbourhood design as
well. Multiple, nearby public social gathering spaces (e.g. cafés and pubs) promote frequent
visits (Oldenburg 1999; Becker 2007). Third places ‒ places excluding work and home ‒
encompass cafés, pubs, neighbourhood streets, greeneries, etc. support casual encounters
and social gathering (Oldenburg 1999). They are technically public space, but regular visitors
develop a sense of ownership like residents do in successful semi-public spaces.
neighbourhood streets (as opposed to major urban streets) have long been premium com-
munity spaces which high traffic speed and volume can harm (Jacobs 1961; appleyard 1981;
Gehl 2010). Car-oriented planning can build a barrier to third and neighbourhood places.
The impacts of such design are probably greater for those who are more mobility-restricted
such as adolescents and the elderly (Boyd 2014). Traffic and traffic noise were prime moti-
vators for high-traffic street residents’ residential relocations, whereas low-traffic street res-
idents factored into housing and neighbourhood qualities (appleyard 1981). This explains
why suburban streets are often perceived as unsafe and unappealing for walking or play,
failing to serve as semi-public space.
Counterintuitively, third places and other urban public space can also be where people
can escape to be alone (Cattell et al. 2008). ability to escape from environmental stressors
may be especially critical for those who live in a crowded house. Therefore, designers and
planners are advised to consider facilitating both social interaction and opportunities to be
alone and restore, even when in a crowd. In addition to close physical proximity to third

Urban street and landscape design
Few studies have examined the connections between building design and outdoor sur-
roundings. views to nature are beneficial in many settings, including indoors (Kaplan, Kaplan,
and ryan 1998, chapter 5). Children from low-income urban families who moved from
poor-quality housing to new single-family houses that had better access to nature showed
improved cognitive functioning (Wells 2000). natural elements (e.g. trees, sound of water)
and aesthetically-pleasing streets can mitigate unpleasant urban sounds (raimbault and
dubois 2005).
While driving and public transportation can be stressful, walking and cycling are rated
positively (Gatersleben and Uzzell 2007). Well-designed landscape and street design can
also enhance walking and cycling journeys (see Gehl 2010, chapter 4.9 for creating bicy-
cling-friendly cities). This is important not only for commuting but also for more frequent
visits to third places. Greater accessibility to outdoors and third places can break the length
of exposure to crowding and noise.

Conclusion
This paper summarizes research on the effects of crowding and noise on human health and
behaviour. Physiological responses (e.g. blood pressure and cortisol levels) indicate these
are stressors. Household crowding and high-rise residential buildings result in negative psy-
chological and behavioural outcomes, including undermining sense of community, and
high classroom density interferes with young students’ academic achievement. Moreover,
high density in residential or classroom settings can reduce parental as well as teacher
responsiveness and engagement with children. In turn, these shifts in adult caregiver behav-
iours can mediate negative outcomes of crowding among children. Second, chronic noise
can interfere with cognitive performance (e.g. memory) and young children’s cognitive
development. Human-environment relations are dynamic and interdependent. For example,
people experiencing crowding tend to withdraw from social interaction to cope with it.
Insufficient auditory privacy may not only increase noise levels but also decrease face-to-face
social interaction, particularly when interrupting others and/or communicating information
that a person would rather others not hear. The timing of exposure to noise and crowding
can be more of concern when designing some building types such as residential, daycare
and K-12 school settings. In addition, this paper has noted carryover effects across settings
and indirect impacts using Bronfenbrenner’s framework. For example, children who attend
crowded daycare and reside in a crowded home appear to suffer worse performance than
if only one setting is crowded.
The present literature review discussed the harmful impacts of crowding and noise.
Building from this, this paper has also shown examples of good urban and neighbourhood
design that can buffer such negative effects. First, good acoustic design can minimize sound
transmission and optimize sound reverberation time, lessening noise and potentially, crowd-
ing. Second, immediate access to semi-public space or third places can reduce noise and
crowding and is critical especially for coping with residential crowding. Third, natural ele-
ments, aesthetically-pleasing and pedestrian-friendly urban design, and safe streets for
walking and bicycling can mitigate crowding and urban noise from both indoor and outdoor
settings. In addition, they can help break the duration of continuous noise and crowding
exposure.
It should be noted that exposure to multiple stressors can exacerbate negative conse-
quences. Many studies show that exposure to multiple stressors can have additive, adverse
consequences (Evans, li, and Whipple 2013). although the physical qualities of neighbour-
hoods and housing are both capable of engendering stress in people, recent work shows
that the two interact (Jones-rounds, Evans, and Braubach 2014). Poor quality housing in a
poor quality neighbourhood produces significantly more stress than either alone. Few stud-
ies have looked into such interaction between interior and exterior environments.
a holistic approach that incorporates dynamic interactions among people, culture and
organizations, and the physical settings that support them can lead to better understanding
of human-environment processes. design that is wondrous to the senses and comprehends
a human- ecological context is what designers and inhabitants ought to expect.
